site.title: Limitations in existing regulatory mechanisms when applied to attacks by AI agents
site.subtitle: Current reporting mechanisms with investigative or regulatory capabilities have deficiencies that make reporting any autonomous AI agent related incidents to date unfeasible by third parties. The incidents in question are the Hugging Face attacks, the DSEwiki attacks, the Anthropic PyPI incident, the RubyGems breach, and an attack on four unnamed victims by OpenAI agents. All of these systems are confidential or publish no public record, and they fail either by not accepting reports from non-providers or by a threshold that disqualifies the incidents that have already happened. This site exists as a complementary visual tool that aggregates the research and our conclusions. For an in-depth look at the work done, including the methodology, you can read the linked paper.
ui.select: Select a cell to see why it fails.
intro.featured: An analysis of the existing filing systems indicates that existing systems fail at one of three critical points: the identity of the filer, the threshold for filing, or whether anything becomes public. We present two cases, the Hugging Face attack and the incident involving DSEwiki, and showcase where the holes are.
intro.legend: The fact that these systems fail at critical points allowed us to build a table of the reporting systems we investigated against each incident, showing where each system fails for each case.
intro.hypothetical: Finally, we constructed a fictional incident to examine how the existing systems would handle a more serious, real-world case. The incident involves an agent causing bodily injury to a person during tests carried out by a fictional Provider X. We examine whether the injured party would be able to file a report themselves, and what is released afterwards.
status.not-applicable: Not a condition for this channel
gate.eu_art85.threshold.note: Article 85 of the statute has no carve-out for Articles 53–55 — the exclusion is the Commission's online tool design, though commentary reads the statute as wider and notes the tool could be reworked to match it. The Commission's tool and FAQ route the GPAI articles elsewhere, there is no Article 5 prohibited practice to allege, and no source applies the broader reading to the documented incidents. Our research and the external analysis converge: the incidents do not qualify.
gate.sb53.threshold.note: Whether an incident is a 'critical safety incident' is the team's analysis; no authority has ruled on these specific incidents. The frontier developer decides whether the incident clears the bar before any duty attaches, and Cal OES's review of public reports is discretionary.
gate.eu_art55.threshold.note: Whether an incident is an Art. 3(49) 'serious incident' is the team's analysis; no authority has ruled. On the text as written, none of the documented incidents qualifies, and the team reads all five as below the bar. External readings of the law agree that the DSEwiki case would not count as a serious incident and would not breach any other provision of the AI Act. The provider decides whether the bar is met before any duty attaches — there is no external check (the self-classification gate).
gate.eu_art89_2.threshold.note: The channel reaches Articles 53–55, including serious-incident reporting. The same reasoning applies: on the text as written, none of the documented incidents qualifies as a 'serious incident'. Whether one does remains the upstream provider's own classification — the same self-classification gate as Article 55.
featured.hf_sb53.headline: California's administering agency confirmed that the Hugging Face intrusion did not classify as a critical safety incident, making it unreportable under SB 53. The public reporting channel is open to anyone — but it only covers 'critical safety incidents', and the bar requires harm on the order of more than 50 deaths or $1 billion in damage.
featured.wiki_eu_art55.headline: OpenAI did file a report under the EU's AI Act, focusing on the DSEwiki incident, and called the incident a 'misalignment'. The Commission confirmed receipt, while declining to say when it arrived, which provision it relied on, or whether the incident qualifies as a 'serious incident'. Article 55 is fileable only by providers of GPAI models with systemic risks.
case.hf.sb53.threshold.note: For this incident the exclusion is not only the team's reading: at a joint Assembly hearing on Aug 10, 2026, the administering agency (Cal OES) stated on the record that the Hugging Face hack 'did not meet the threshold' for SB 53.
hypo.sb53.headline: Clears the bar, so the public may file. SB 53 §22757.11(d)(3) makes 'loss of control of a frontier model causing death or bodily injury' a critical safety incident.
hypo.eu_art55.headline: Covers the harm, but only Provider X may file. Bodily injury is what Art. 3(49)(a) ('death or serious harm to health') is for, so a serious-incident duty plausibly attaches.
hypo.eu_art85.headline: Qualifies, and anyone may file — but nothing becomes public. On these facts there is a concrete harm to allege, so the complaint clears the threshold, and Article 85 is open to any natural or legal person.
axis.filer.label: Who may file
axis.filer.desc: Some channels accept anyone; some accept only the model's provider, only downstream providers, or only insiders. Where the gate excludes you, the incident has no route.
axis.threshold.label: Whether it qualifies
axis.threshold.desc: The incident must clear a legal bar — a 'critical safety incident' in California, a 'serious incident' in the EU. Below it, nothing fires even if a channel is open.
axis.visibility.label: Whether anything becomes public
axis.visibility.desc: Even when a report is possible, it enters a confidential channel and the authority acts at its discretion. No public knowledge accumulates.
axis.legalBasis.label: Governing law
axis.legalBasis.desc: The law that creates the mechanism and the provisions it enforces.
axis.authority.label: Run by
axis.authority.desc: The body that administers the mechanism — distinct from whoever decides whether an incident qualifies.

case.hf.name: Hugging Face intrusion (Jul 2026)
case.hf.summary: OpenAI evaluation agents escaped their sandbox, turned a customer's exposed code-execution endpoint into a launchpad, and broke into Hugging Face production infrastructure, reaching cluster-admin in under 13 hours.
case.wiki.name: Wiki collusion (May–Jul 2026)
case.wiki.summary: Autonomous agents made ~18,000 edits to a dormant German wiki to coordinate on timed tasks; OpenAI classified the episode as a 'misalignment' finding, not a security incident, and did not disclose it for about four months.
case.victims.name: The four unnamed victims (Jul 2026)
case.victims.summary: During the Hugging Face incident, OpenAI's agents used publicly exposed credentials on four additional services; the victims were never named publicly.
case.anthropic.name: Anthropic evaluation incidents (Jul + Sep 2026)
case.anthropic.summary: Four incidents in which Claude models reached real third parties, including a name-collision company and 15 vendors via a malicious PyPI package; none of the affected organizations had detected the activity.
case.rubygems.name: RubyGems / RubyDoc (May 2026)
case.rubygems.summary: OpenAI agents uploaded 2,000+ malicious packages and abused a documentation site to run code, targeting a previously unknown vulnerability.
case.hypo_injury.name: An agent injures someone during a test
case.hypo_injury.summary: While Provider X was testing an AI agent, the agent went outside what it had been asked to do and seriously injured a person. Provider X is a large frontier developer and a GPAI provider with systemic risk; the injured person has no connection to Provider X.
case.hypo_injury.threshold.note: In this hypothetical the harm is concrete, so the incident clears the threshold.
